newsitem.title: USA: Sprint says competition forced rate cuts.
newsitem.headline: Sprint says competition forced rate cuts.

text.p: Sprint Corp on Monday became the latest long-distance telephone company to cut international rates in the face of stepped-up competition.

"It's simply competition," Daniel Alcazar, director of international marketing for Sprint's Consumer Services Group. "With the prices dropping, to remain competitive we're simply forced into a situation where we have to remain viable in the marketplace, and to do that we have to be price competitive."

Sprint said it cut its weekend international rates as part of the Sprint Sense International calling plan. Weekend calls to Britain will cost $0.10 a minute, or the same as a domestic U.S. call, and calls to Germany, Italy and France will cost $0.30 a minute.
Calls are more expensive during the week, and Alcazar said some price increases also took effect on weekdays.

Sprint said about half of its international long-distance traffic came between midnight Friday and midnight Sunday. It said U.S. consumers made about 2.8 billion international calls in 1995, totaling about 16 billion minutes.

In January, AT&T Corp, which is said to hold the largest share of the residential long-distance market, initiated its AT&T One Rate International plan, which offers a permanent flat rate for calls to each country. It offers calls to Britain at $0.12 a minute, and calls to Germany, France or Italy at $0.35..

Since January, MCI Communications Corp has charged a flat residential rate of $0.12 a minute for calls to Britain, if the customer spends at least $25 a month in long distance. Customers are entitled to the same rate when using a calling card or receiving a collect call, the company said.
The flat rate for Germany and France is $0.35 a minute, and all calls are charged in six-second increments.

"This really is a result of the cost that we pay carriers in other countries to handle the switch on their ends," Brad Burns, a spokesman for MCI, said. "It really is about these overseas markets opening to competition, and competition drives down the settlement rates. It's all the function of a very healthy competitive market."
All three companies charge a monthly fee of $3.00 for their international plans.
Sprint said it did not expect the calling plan to have a material impact on revenues because the number of international minutes it booked should increase.
"It's an adjustment by one company to a competitive reality," said Sam Peltzman, a professor of economics at the University of Chicago's Graduate School of Business.
Peltzman said there was excess international long-distance capacity on the networks because all three major companies have built high-tech networks.
"The extra cost for carrying a call approaches zero," Peltzman said. "There is no sort of natural floor to how low these prices can go."
Sprint said it had other calling plans in the works though not all of them were based on price.

"The industry is going to become increasingly focused on coming up with new product concepts," Alcazar said. "At some point it doesn't make sense to be in business if all we're going to do is drive our prices down to single digits. Nobody will make money."
